title: Reception Second Term
overview: 1. Second-Term Curriculum Intent Reception First Term established SETTLE -> SECURE -> DECODE -> REPRESENT -> REASON. Second Term progresses towards DEEPEN -> READ -> COMPOSE -> INVESTIGATE -> APPLY. Children use increasingly secure foundations for systematic synthetic phonics, word reading and fluency, language comprehension, sentence composition, handwriting, number composition and reasoning, scientific enquiry, knowledge of people/places/nature, creative thinking, self-regulation and independent learning. RECEPTION REMAINS EARLY YEARS. 2. First Term to Second Term Progression First Term Second Term Progression Settle into Reception Manage routines increasingly independently Recognise taught graphemes Recall and apply taught correspondences Begin blending Blend increasingly automatically Read simple decodable words Read increasingly complex matched text Segment orally Segment increasingly for spelling Write labels/captions Compose increasingly complete sentences Understand small quantities Explore number composition deeply Compare quantities Reason about number relationships Notice patterns Explain and create patterns Explore shape and space Apply spatial reasoning Observe Predict and investigate Answer questions Explain reasoning increasingly Cooperative play Sustained collaborative projects Manage belongings Manage learning resources Progression: KNOW -> PRACTISE -> APPLY -> EXPLAIN -> DEEPEN 3. Second-Term Curriculum Map Week Big Idea Main Development 1 Back Together - Ready to Learn Reconnection, routines and assessment 2 People Who Help Us Community, occupations and service 3 Journeys and Transport Movement, maps, routes and comparison 4 Materials and Their Properties Investigation and descriptive language 5 Forces - Push, Pull and Movement Prediction, cause and effect 6 Consolidation / Calendar Flexibility Responsive review 7 Animals and Their Environments Classification, habitats and care 8 Plants, Food and Growth Living things, food origins and change 9 Number Relationships Composition, comparison and reasoning 10 Measure, Shape and Spatial Thinking Mathematical application 11 Machines, Technology and How Things Work Technology, systems and responsibility 12 Stories From Nigeria and the World Comprehension, narrative and culture 13 What Can I Explain Now? Consolidation, application and reflection Week 1 - Back Together: Ready to Learn Reconnect after the holiday and re-establish learning behaviours. Develop recounting and sequencing language; re-establish routines, relationships, self-regulation and independence; revisit phonics according to the adopted programme and assess grapheme recall, oral/word blending, segmenting and decodable reading; revisit subitising, counting, cardinality, composition, comparison and pattern; resume Practical Life responsibilities. Character: Responsibility and Readiness. Week 2 - People Who Help Us Progress from naming occupations towards role -> tool -> responsibility -> service. Explore teachers, healthcare workers, farmers, traders, drivers, builders, security workers, cleaners, emergency workers and locally relevant roles without gender stereotyping. Use fiction/non-fiction, lists, labels, captions, messages, role-play records and practical mathematics. Root examples in Owo and children's families. Character: SERVICE. Week 3 - Journeys and Transport Investigate movement of people/goods and increasingly represent journeys. Vocabulary includes journey, route, destination, transport, passenger, vehicle, map, direction and distance. Compare road/water/rail/air transport without rote classification; develop positional language, simple maps, labels/captions, oral directions, obstacle routes and age-appropriate road safety. Begin with transport children genuinely encounter. Character: Patience and Responsibility. Week 4 - Materials and Their Properties Investigate why materials suit different purposes. Vocabulary includes material, property, transparent, waterproof, absorbent, flexible, rigid, strong, weak, rough and smooth. Safely investigate wood, metal, plastic, paper, card, fabric, rubber and adult-managed glass contexts. Ask which material works best and why; use information texts, investigation records, sorting/classifying and intentional construction. Character: Curiosity and Wise Choice. Week 5 - Forces: Push, Pull and Movement Investigate movement and early cause/effect through cars on ramps, balls, surfaces, pushing, pulling, rolling, sliding and ramp height. Adult vocabulary may include force, friction, speed, surface, ramp and steep without requiring formal definitions. Scientific thinking: QUESTION -> PREDICT -> TRY -> OBSERVE -> TALK. Compare/order distances and record observations. Character: Curiosity and Perseverance. Week 6 - Consolidation / Calendar Flexibility No formal examination. Review phonics, decodable reading, comprehension, writing, number, mathematical reasoning, communication, PSED, physical development, investigation and Practical Life. Determine graphemes to revisit, blending automaticity, reading support, secure number concepts, language support and intervention effectiveness. ASSESS TO IMPROVE TEACHING. Week 7 - Animals and Their Environments Develop increasingly systematic knowledge of animals, habitats and basic needs. Compare features, movement, food, young, habitat and needs; introduce useful classification vocabulary naturally and avoid false rules such as 'all birds fly'. Read animal stories/information texts, write labels/captions/simple facts, sort by varied criteria, compare quantity/size and create habitats/models. Character: Care and Stewardship. Week 8 - Plants, Food and Growth Connect plants, growth, farming, food and human needs. Plant and observe; compare growth; discuss plant needs and food origins. Use locally meaningful crops such as yam, cassava, maize, beans, rice, plantain, vegetables and fruits. Measure informally, sequence/count/represent observations, read farming texts, draw/write observations and provide safe food preparation. Character: Gratitude, Patience and Stewardship. Week 9 - Number Relationships Deepen composition, comparison, subitising, one more/one fewer, informal equal groups, part-whole relationships and number bonds through practical experience. Explore numbers such as 5 in multiple compositions using objects, fingers, images and play before symbolic recording dominates. Ask 'How do you know?', 'Can you show it another way?', 'What changed?' and 'Is there another possibility?'. MATHEMATICAL DEPTH BEFORE SPEED. Week 10 - Measure, Shape and Spatial Thinking Apply mathematical language to length, height, weight, capacity, time/sequence, 2D shapes, 3D objects, properties, rotation, shape composition, maps, puzzles, routes and position. Use real problems such as comparing containers, stabilising towers and composing pictures with shapes. Practical Life includes pouring, transferring, arranging and everyday measuring. Character: Accuracy, Patience and Persistence. Week 11 - Machines, Technology and How Things Work Develop age-appropriate understanding that technology is designed for purposes. Explore safe familiar technology such as torch, clock, fan, telephone, camera, computer, keyboard, mechanical devices and programmable resources where available. Children may photograph, draw digitally, type selected characters, listen to recordings and follow simple digital instructions. CHILDREN SHOULD USE TECHNOLOGY - NOT SIMPLY CONSUME SCREENS. Introduce ask-an-adult, privacy and stop/tell safety. Character: Wisdom and Responsibility. Week 12 - Stories From Nigeria and the World Deepen comprehension and narrative through Nigerian stories, Yoruba oral stories where appropriate, African literature, traditional tales, modern picture books and stories from other cultures. Predict, infer simply, retell, sequence, compare characters, explain preferences and ask questions; create stories through oral storytelling, drawing, maps, role play, shared and independent writing. African stories should also represent modern childhood, towns, cities and technology. Character: Wisdom, Respect and Imagination. Week 13 - What Can I Explain Now? Consolidate through explanation/application rather than conventional examinations. Revisit phonics, decodable books, stories, writing, number, mathematical challenges, investigations, construction, technology, Practical Life and outdoor learning. Ask what the child can now explain/apply independently, what remains insecure and what Third Term should prioritise. 4. Second-Term Phonics & Reading Continue the adopted systematic synthetic phonics programme with new grapheme-phoneme correspondences according to sequence, cumulative review, oral blending, word blending, segmenting, spelling, programme-aligned tricky/common exception words and decodable reading. Independent phonics-practice books must be closely matched to taught knowledge. Children should increasingly decode rather than guess from pictures, first letters or context; pictures support meaning and enjoyment. 5. Reading Comprehension Develop comprehension through rich vocabulary, read-aloud stories, conversation, prediction, retelling, questioning, simple inference, sequencing and discussion. AMES maintains both BOOKS CHILDREN CAN READ and BOOKS CHILDREN CAN EXPERIENCE. 6. Second-Term Writing Progression Writing connects ORAL LANGUAGE -> PHONICS -> HANDWRITING -> COMPOSITION. Children increasingly say sentences, segment words, represent sounds with taught graphemes, form letters, use increasingly appropriate spacing and write labels, captions, messages, lists, simple sentences and story-related text. Adult support should preserve the child's composition. 7. Handwriting Teach posture, stable seating, paper position, effective pencil grip, fine-motor strength, correct movement patterns and accurate formation of taught graphemes systematically. QUALITY OF FORMATION BEFORE QUANTITY OF COPYING. 8. Mathematics - Second-Term Progression Deepen subitising, cardinality, composition, comparison, numerical patterns, one more/one fewer, number relationships and practical problem-solving alongside rich shape, space, measure, pattern and construction. Manipulatives remain important. Progression: CONCRETE -> IMAGE -> LANGUAGE -> SYMBOL. 9. Communication and Language Language development remains whole-curriculum. Adults model precise vocabulary, complete explanations, reasoning/story/comparative/time/scientific/mathematical language and prompts such as 'Explain how you know', 'What changed?' and 'Can you describe it another way?' 10. Practical Life - Second Term First Term: I CAN MANAGE MYSELF AND MY LEARNING. Second Term: I CAN TAKE RESPONSIBILITY FOR MY LEARNING ENVIRONMENT. Children increasingly prepare/restore resources, organise workspaces, care for equipment, serve, pour, clean, fold, sort, manage belongings and complete responsibilities. Adults avoid doing automatically what children can increasingly do. 11. Continuous Provision Continue Reading, Writing, Mathematics, Construction, Small World, Role Play, Creative Arts, Investigation, Technology, Practical Life, Fine Motor and Outdoor Learning. Provision evolves into academically powerful experiences: e.g., transport can include map-making, ticket writing, route planning, vehicle construction, distance comparison and journey storytelling rather than merely toy cars. 12. Outdoor Learning Use movement, routes, maps, ramps, forces, distance, measurement, planting, weather, animal/minibeast observation, large construction, phonics trails, word hunts, storytelling, mathematical games and collaborative challenges intentionally. 13. Christian Character Spine Develop Responsibility, Service, Patience, Curiosity, Perseverance, Care, Stewardship, Gratitude, Wisdom, Respect and Imagination through classroom life, adult modelling and reflection. 14. Inclusion & SEND Ask WHAT IS THE BARRIER TO LEARNING? Support may include additional phonics practice, language modelling, vocabulary pre-teaching, visual prompts, smaller groups, sensory adaptation, movement breaks, adapted writing tools, alternative communication, repeated reading, manipulatives and adult scaffolding. Increase access without unnecessarily reducing intellectual opportunity. 15. Parent Partnership Give clear guidance on phonics pronunciation, blending, reading practice, book routines, handwriting, meaningful writing, number games and independence. Avoid conflicting phonics methods. Home reading includes both matched child-practice books and enjoyable adult read-aloud books. 16. Second-Term Assessment Monitor all EYFS areas with particular attention to phonics recall, blending, decodable reading, comprehension, segmenting, writing, letter formation, number composition, subitising, comparison, mathematical reasoning, language, self-regulation and independence. Assessment must produce action; e.g., grapheme recognition without blending leads to increased oral/word-blending practice, not merely more evidence collection. 17. End-of-Second-Term Expectations Depending on starting points, children increasingly communicate confidently; listen/respond; use richer vocabulary; retell/discuss stories; apply phonics; blend increasingly automatically; read matched decodable material; segment for spelling; write increasingly complete meaningful sentences; form letters accurately; understand composition; subitise/compare/reason; apply shape/measure language; predict/investigate/describe results; understand communities; compare animals/plants/materials; use technology purposefully; collaborate; manage resources; persist and take responsibility. These are developmental curriculum expectations, not rigid pass/fail criteria. 18. Progression Into Third Term First Term: SETTLE -> SECURE -> DECODE -> REPRESENT -> REASON. Second Term: DEEPEN -> READ -> COMPOSE -> INVESTIGATE -> APPLY. Third Term: FLUENCY -> INDEPENDENCE -> CONNECTION -> REFLECTION -> TRANSITION, continuing phonics, fluency, comprehension, independent composition, story writing, mathematical reasoning, number relationships, problem-solving, nature/change, Nigeria/Africa/world knowledge, collaborative projects, EYFS consolidation, transition profiling and Basic 1 readiness. Reception Second-Term Declaration We will deepen rather than rush. We will teach phonics systematically, practise towards automaticity, read decodable books and wonderful books children cannot yet read themselves, expand vocabulary, compose sentences orally, write for meaning, develop handwriting carefully, teach number relationships, ask children to explain, investigate materials and movement, care for living things, understand community, use technology purposefully, create, collaborate, solve problems, maintain continuous provision, go outdoors, strengthen independence, identify barriers, work with parents, maintain Nigerian identity, widen children's understanding of the world and live Christian character. DEPTH IS NOT THE SAME AS DIFFICULTY. READERS - WRITERS - MATHEMATICAL THINKERS - INVESTIGATORS - COMMUNICATORS - CREATORS - RESPONSIBLE LEARNERS - INDEPENDENT THINKERS HOW DOES THIS HELP THE CHILD FLOURISH? IN GOD WE TRUST.
